paras: The mob attack on M. M. Wadkins took place in Tampa, Florida, on the night of July 31, 1903, when masked men surrounded the house of Wadkins, a Black tailor, and shot him twice as he fled. Wadkins survived by taking refuge on the roof of another house, and police then guarded him. Wire reports presented it as the second mob attack in Tampa in two nights.

The attack came the night after a mob dealt with George Houston, a hackman in Tampa. Wadkins, described as "a colored tailor" living on the city's principal street, was suspected of "criminal intimacy with white women," which the Savannah text called "the same offense" for which Houston had been attacked.

On the night of July 31, "another party of masked men" surrounded Wadkins's house and, according to the dispatch, tried to treat him as Houston had been treated. Wadkins ran, and the mob shot him twice, once in the chin and once through the leg. He burst into the residence of A. J. Knight, "a prominent citizen," and reached the roof before the household realized what had happened.

After the mob dispersed, a detail of police was assigned to protect Wadkins, who offered a $500 reward for the arrest of his attackers. The coverage does not report any arrest, inquiry or later proceedings.

The story reached the white press as a single Tampa telegraph that ran on August 1, 1903, in the Savannah Morning News and the New-York Tribune. The Savannah paper ran it on its front page as "Another Tampa Mob Assails a Negro," with Wadkins's reward offer in the subhead. The Tribune headlined it "Chased Negro and Shot Him," adding "He Would Not Wait to See What Florida Mob Wanted." Both repeated the suspicion against Wadkins without naming its source or commenting on the mob.
No coverage of the attack was found in the Black press.

The two printings of the same dispatch differ on the suspicion against Wadkins: the Savannah Morning News gave "criminal intimacy with white women," while the New-York Tribune gave "assaulting white women."

reader.title: Mob attack on M. M. Wadkins
bases: A party of masked men surrounded Wadkins's house and shot and wounded him as he fled; the reports say they meant to treat him as George Houston had been treated the night before, and no death or stated intent to kill appears (A2, A3).

Wadkins was shot twice but survived under police protection, so no one was killed (A2, A3); the attackers were an unlawful 'party of masked men' of unstated size acting on a suspicion about white women (A2, A3), which makes this an attempted mob attack rather than a lynching.
Both reports carry the same Tampa telegraph text with only small wording differences, so they are one source, not two independent ones (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Tampa wire report
accounts.gist: Masked men surrounded Wadkins's house and shot him twice as he fled into A. J. Knight's house and onto the roof; the mob dispersed and police now guard him. He was suspected of sexual relations with, or assaults on, white women, depending on the version.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran the wire under 'Another Tampa Mob Assails a Negro', tying it to the Houston attack and repeating the suspicion of 'criminal intimacy with white women' without comment.
The New-York Tribune headlined it 'Chased Negro and Shot Him' with the deck 'He Would Not Wait to See What Florida Mob Wanted', and gave the suspicion as 'assaulting white women'.

versions.value: suspected of criminal intimacy with white women, 'the same offense for which Houston was dealt with'

conflicts.note: Both texts come from the same telegraph; the Savannah wording is longer and links the suspicion to the Houston case, while the Tribune's shorter version describes it as assault. Neither gives any source for the suspicion.
